quotes.text: A composer in his own right, Emerson was famous for taking modern composers like Joplin, Mussorgsky, Brubeck, Copland and Ginastera and making their music his own, exposing many to artists they may not have heard of.

He also was no stranger to stabbing knives into his keyboards during performances of "Rondo" and "America," as well as taking endless solos on multiple keyboards – in short, embodying the excesses and entertainment that was progressive rock.
The Works project had drained the trio creatively, and so this disc amounts to a much lesser rehash than Works Vol. 1.
Rather than try to retool their sound for the '80s like Yes and Genesis, ELP simply called it a day after 1978.
For better or worse, the guys opted against the long songs and pretension of their heyday, instead condensing their attack into shorter, punchier songs.
Emerson's variety of keyboard textures, solos that alternate between bombast and hypnotic, and a very strong emphasis on melody and momentum throughout make this feel a lot faster than its runtime.
After the group formed in the spring of 1970, they entered rehearsals and prepared material for an album which became a mix of original songs and rock arrangements of classical music.

"Take a Pebble" was written by Lake, with the primary sections being a jazz keyboard arrangement by Emerson, and the middle section being a folk guitar work by Lake with water-like percussion effects from Palmer, plus bits of clapping and whistling.

"Knife-Edge" is based on the first movement of Leoš Janáček's orchestral piece Sinfonietta (1926), with an instrumental middle section that includes an extended quotation from the Allemande of Johann Sebastian Bach's first French Suite No. 1 in D minor, BWV 812, but played on an organ rather than a clavichord or piano.

"The Three Fates" is a three-part "pseudo suite", written and predominantly performed by Emerson. Each section is named after the three sisters of Greek mythology known as the three Three Fates (or Moirai).
This opens with 'The Barbarian,' a keyboard showpiece (not to slight all the flailing and booming underneath) replete with the shifts of tempo, time, key, and dynamics beloved of these bozos.
